audited_plan.image_description: A male Mallard duck (drake) swimming in water. The bird features a characteristic iridescent green head, a white neck ring, a yellow bill, and a grey/brown body. It is positioned in profile facing left.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The bill is present and structurally correct (broad/flat), but the color is a vibrant, solid yellow. The checkpoint specifies 'dark grey to yellow-green'. While Mallards can have yellowish bills, this specific shade deviates from the provided textual definition of the class.
The eye is clearly visible against the green plumage and appears black/dark brown, matching the description.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The body shape is anatomically correct for a duck, sitting high in the water (buoyant) with a smooth, streamlined silhouette.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The image perfectly matches the 'Mallard' pattern described: iridescent green head, distinct white neck ring, and grey/brown body feathers.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The duck is swimming, and its legs/feet are completely submerged and occluded by the water surface. They are genuinely impossible to see.
The folded wing is visible on the side of the body, showing the correct broad shape and tapering towards the tail.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The characteristic upward curl of the central tail feathers (speculum area) is visible at the rear of the duck.

artifact_observations.reasoning: The water ripples immediately adjacent to the duck's breast show slight smearing and lack of sharp displacement physics, appearing slightly 'painted on' rather than physically interacting with the hull.
The very tip of the yellow bill appears slightly flattened and lacks the crisp 3D volume seen in the rest of the head, suggesting minor generation artifacting at the extremity.
